This 1977 Ford F-150 Entered the Shop With a V8 Under the Hood, Drove Out With a Tesla Motor
11 photos
Photo: Scotten Motors | YouTube
This 1977 Ford F-150 left stock days far behind for a gas-free life following a "heart" transplant. Instead of a roaring factory V8 engine, it now has the quiet Tesla powertrain, a custom 100-kWh battery pack, and the attitude that would have made the discontinued Ford F-150 Lightning EV jealous.
While others modify sixth-gen Ford F-150s into sky-high show-off trucks , Scott from Scotten Motors converted one into an EV by transplanting a Tesla Model S Small Drive Unit (SDU) into his truck. The unit is rated at 295 horsepower and 245 pound-feet in factory configuration, but the team softwared it down to 264 horsepower during the project’s initial testing phase.
However, right now, on the Scotten Motors EV Builds specification sheet, the rebuilt Tesla SDU package is officially rated at 295 horsepower and 245 pound-feet of torque, while it is controlled via a Dynam Labs VCU+ motor controller. The motor is mounted out back, directly to the frame between the rear wheels, on a De Dion axle setup, and sends power to the wheels via CV joints and chromoly half-axles.
The truck now sports a custom 85-kWh battery pack, using 16 Tesla Model S modules split into three main custom-machined enclosures from AMP Revolt, wired in series, with ten modules sitting inside the engine bay, where the V8 used to be, and six modules running along the old transmission tunnel and where the driveshaft used to be.
Photo: Scotten Motors | YouTube Scott mentions a 350-cubic-inch Windsor V8 came out of the truck, though Ford never actually built a 350 Windsor. Instead, Ford offered a 351-cubic-inch (5.8-liter) Windsor V8 in Mustangs, passenger cars, and later 1980s - 1990s F-150s. While the 1977 F-150 did offer a 351 V8 producing 156 horsepower (158 metric horsepower), it was the taller-deck 351M engine.
The most powerful version of the F-150 in 1977 was the one with the 460-cubic-inch V8 under the hood, pushing out 220 horsepower (223 metric horsepower), which is still very much behind what the Tesla motor can do right now.
The battery is managed via a Dilithium BMS and a custom house-built contactor box. Scott gets roughly 220 to 230 miles (354 kilometers to 370 kilometers) of range before he needs to plug his F-150 in again. The truck uses a 7-kW Level 2 charger but has no DC fast charging.
Because the battery layout mirrors the front-to-center weight distribution of the actual ICE-powered truck, the total weight is only about 40 pounds (18 kilograms) over the stock weight. The F-150 retains its original front suspension, payload, and towing capacity.
Photo: Scotten Motors | YouTube Scott replaced the front braking system, fitting the vehicle with Wilwood disc brakes. He also came up with an upgraded steering column and installed electric power steering. The vehicle features a coolant-based heating system, drawn from a dedicated reservoir with its own water pump, tied into a vintage-style Classic Auto Air blower unit.
The cabin heater pulls warm coolant from a dedicated electric loop into the concealed Classic Auto Air blower unit, keeping the original dashboard controls operational while running much quieter than the 1977 fan. And yes, all original 1977 analog gauges stood their ground in the cabin, where Scott installed a stock-looking retro radio, which features wireless Apple CarPlay.
Why did Scott go for a 1977 Ford F-150? It brings back childhood memories. He grew up in the 1980s and 90s in a sixth-generation Ford on the Delmarva Peninsula. That is what everyone had because nobody could afford a new one. Now, one of those trucks rolls quietly and makes no stops at the gas station just like the F-150 Lightning that Ford pulled the plug on nearly a year ago.

EICMA 2026 • Here Are Some of the Serious and Obscure Brands That EICMA 2026 Had To Offer – Worth Knowing About
Volkswagen ID.4-Replacing ID. Tiguan Starts Production at Emden Plant in Germany
81 photos
Photo: Volkswagen
Europe's largest automaker by global sales has recently started assembling the ID. Tiguan. Hailing from the Emden factory in northern Germany, the zero-emission model doesn't replace only the ID.4 crossover. For model year 2027, the ID.5 isn't coming back due to sluggish demand across European markets.
Volkswagen says that ID. Tiguan deliveries will begin in the earliest part of 2027. This crossover couldn't have arrived at a more awkward moment for the Emden complex, which faces an uncertain future under the Wolfsburg-based manufacturer's latest restructuring plan.
The ID. Tiguan will be launching in three powertrain configurations, split between rear-wheel drive and 4MOTION dual-motor AWD. Production output should increase gradually over the coming weeks. Adopting more conventional styling than the ID.4, the newcomer benefits from a more upright front end, more pronounced surfaces, and pull-type handles instead of the flush nonsense from before.
Volkswagen has also addressed the problem regarding physical controls, which now replace some of the previous touch-sensitive arrangements. Its dashboard combines a 10-inch digital instrument cluster with a 15-inch central touchscreen, and there's also an optional 12-inch passenger display that needs highlighting.
Gifted with a small front storage compartment, the ID. Tiguan is listed with 534 liters (18.8 cubic feet) of storage capacity behind the rear seats. Folding them flat into the floor gets you 1,577 liters, namely 55.7 cubic feet where metric speak is frowned upon. The base rear-drive specification uses a 58-kWh battery of the LFP variety and a drive unit that outputs 187 horsepower.
Photo: Volkswagen The most you can ask of it with a full charge is 450 kilometers (280 miles) in the WLTP test cycle, while 100 kilometers per hour (62 miles per hour) is doable in 8.5 seconds. Prospective customers who need more driving range are presented with a 77-kWh pack that employs a nickel-manganese-cobalt chemistry. This battery can be had with either rear- or all-wheel drive.
RWD means 282 horsepower and no more than 600 kilometers (373 miles), with 0-100 estimated at 6.7 seconds. Opting for 4MOTION means 295 horsepower and 560 kilometers (348 miles), with Volkswagen also quoting a 6.1-second sprint to 100 clicks for the European-spec model. Charging-wise, the LFP and NMC batteries can take up to 105 and 165 kilowatts, respectively.
That's 26 or 29 minutes from 10 to 80 percent on direct current, with both versions supporting 11 kilowatts on AC. Available to configure from 42,695 euros in Germany, the ID. Tiguan tows either 1,800 kilograms (3,968 pounds) with the lesser pack or 2,000 kilograms (4,409 pounds) with the larger one.
Volkswagen's Emden facility used to build the Beetle in the 1960s, after which the Passat became its defining product. In preparation for the ID.4, the plant's transition toward electric began in 2020 as part of an investment totaling more than 1 billion euros. More than 500,000 electric vehicles have been produced there since 2022, and the final combustion vehicle left Emden in 2024.
Under the automaker's Future Plan 2030 strategy, Volkswagen cannot guarantee future production allocations for Emden and three additional plants between 2031 and 2034. The Wolfsburg-based colossus has to reduce excess manufacturing capacity in Europe by 500,000 vehicles fast, and more details about Emden's future will be revealed by the end of June 2027.
As it stands, the ID. Tiguan needs to generate sufficient production volume to support a plant whose future is still at play. Whether the Emden complex will be allocated new models in the 2030s, that will partly depend on the commercial success of the compact-sized electric crossover.

EICMA 2026 • Honda CRF1150L Africa Twin Enduro Sports Is a Tongue Twister, Weighs Less but Offers More
The 964 Carrera RS Book Is a Love Letter to Porsche’s ‘90s Sportscar: I Interviewed Its Author
56 photos
Photo: Christoph Mader
In the ‘70s, my dad used to spend what little lunch money he had to buy books. He’d typically have to save up for a week or two to get one title. It was his only way to travel the world and “escape” the rural life with all of its difficult moments. He took good care of those books, and had them all inside several bookshelves inside the house.
It’s no wonder I have always been so fond of reading myself. I was in the fourth grade when I read the Iliad, and the fifth when I started exploring Dune. With hundreds of titles at home, there was no need for me to save up to buy more of them. So I used my daily allowance for scale model cars instead. I’ve bought at least 100 books since going to college though, and they’ll be part of my new home soon.
There’s one title that I didn’t expect I’d get access to so soon though, and it will be one of the highlights of my collection for sure. I’m talking about Christoph Mäder’s Porsche 964 Carrera RS book, which Mäder Morse Field Recordings published in November of 2025. I’m talking about a real love letter to the 964 Carrera RS family, covering six major topics throughout 442 richly illustrated pages.
Even before getting the chance to interview Christoph, I learned that the research process for the book took three and a half years. If that’s not a clear sign of commitment and passion for the subject, I don’t know what is. As with every story that I explore, I am always curious to go straight to its early phase of development.
“I was the first one in my family who liked cars. I was around 15 when I saw Nigel Mansell recovering from a high-speed spin at Imola, and I watched every single F1 race from that moment on. I wanted to get a car as fast as possible so I convinced my brother to buy an Alfa Romeo Alfasud. It had the 95 hp engine, with double carburetors: it wasn’t the best looking car in the world but still felt special."
I used that photo as a reminder Photo: Mäder Morse Field Recordings "It sounded and handled great, and by the time I turned 18 I bought it from my brother. I obviously didn’t forget about F1, and went to my first race in 1992 back when Michael Schumacher won at Spa in the Benetton-Ford car .” I must say that I typically take less than 45 minutes for a complete interview, but I needed twice as much this time as I wanted to learn as much about Christoph’s work and history as possible.
The fact that he had a 1:12th-scale Mazda 787B parked on a piece of furniture behind me obviously required me to ask about it and some of the other diecast models he had. And I was surprised to hear that he didn’t use to collect them as a kid. He was more into model planes at the time, and I guess that could be an interesting topic for one of his future books.
I was itching to learn how he got the Porsche “bug” in the first place, as you can’t delve so deep into the topic without genuinely loving the company and its cars. “I had to play an instrument as a kid, and it was the clarinet. I wasn’t too happy about it but had to do it regardless. As I was going to my teacher’s house for lessons, I noticed the a Porsche 911 Carrera 3.0 parked nearby."
"I had my Polaroid camera with me, and I used that photo as a reminder to keep me motivated through college. When I got my third paycheck, I went to the bank and borrowed the money to buy a 911 SC. I was 27 at the time, and just seven months later I had no tires, no clutch, no brakes and no exhaust and no money to fix any of it. Seven months and almost 40,000 km, and I had to sell it and move on for the time being. It took me 20 years to get the next one.”
We weren’t brave enough to go for two books Photo: Mäder Morse Field Recordings Christoph went through over 20 cars during that period, and it didn’t surprise me to hear several of them were Alfas, too. He even tried a BMW E21, but didn’t enjoy it as much. And I learned that one of his dream machines for the future is an Aston Martin Vantage V8 with a manual gearbox, alongside the Porsche 997 GT3 RS 4.0 of course. While it’s easy to understand why the Porsche is on the list, you might ask what’s up with the Aston Martin.
Well, Christoph used to design liveries for race cars before writing books, and the Jetalliance Racing Aston Martin DBR9 was one of his favorite projects. He even worked on the green Zakspeed Viper back in the day, and a few other vehicles that he also owns diecast replicas of. That’s certainty the next level of flexing for a diecast enthusiast and I might have to continue exploring the topic in a separate story soon.
The career switch came in 2010, when Christoph was asked to undertake a project on the DBR9 for T.A.G Books. “Since I was close to the team, I was there for every test and race, knew all the drivers and team, which means it took me about 18 months to finish writing the book. My next one was about the Carrera RS, and the 911R followed not long after that."
"We weren’t brave enough to go for two books on the latter (one for the older model and one for the new car). That’s how we should’ve done it. With the 911R book we discovered the power of Social Media, and that helped more people get access to our work.” While I’m writing this interview after reading through the 964 Carrera RS book, I must say I am equally curious to get a closer look at some of his other titles on the Porsche 930 Turbo 3.0, the Porsche 993 GT2 and the Porsche 964 Turbo S Lightweight.
I started working on three cars at the same time Photo: Mäder Morse Field Recordings At this rate, I might have to think of a special Porsche corner in my new home. I guess window shopping for my first 911 on elferspot for several hours a week is going to have to stop for a while so I can focus on saving up first. Anyway, with so many different variations of the 911 coming out of Zuffenhausen in the past 60 years, I wanted to know how Christoph selected this one for his newest work.
“I started working on three cars at the same time: the 964 Carrera RS, the 911 GT1 and the 959. It wasn’t that long ago that I realized I didn’t need a bank to finance the cost of producing a book like this, which is how I started Mader Morse Field Recordings. I knew I needed a strong foundation for the new company, and also that Porsche made over 2,000 units of the 964 Carrera RS. That means there are probably more than 2,000 people who own one, which sounded like a good start to me.”
Given that Christoph has interviewed over 40 key figures and eyewitnesses that were involved with the development, design or racing programs associated with the 964 Carrera RS, he’s genuinely got access to an impressive collection of sound files containing information most people might have never had access to before. I told him I’d be the first one to get in line for a chance to see a video/documentary version of the stories he’s working on.
It obviously all boils down to budget issues, as going down that route is a sure way of making things a bit more complicated. Right now, the 964 Carrera RS book is available in English , German, and French and you can opt between the Regular Edition and the Special Edition, with several color options to choose from. I’ll be back with another story with my assessment of it all and more information from Christoph soon as I can hardly cover everything there is to say about it in one go.

EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
Former NBA Star Takes His Mercedes-AMG G 63 to a Tuner, Drives Back in a Different-Looking Ride
11 photos
Photo: Instagram | stars.in.the.ceiling
Did you think that just because the second-generation Mercedes G-Class is some one and a half years away from turning ten that it does not get that much traction in our news feed? Well, obviously not, especially if you are an avid reader, because this model still slides under the spotlight very often.
In fact, is not a single week without us dedicating at least a story to the iconic off-roader for different reasons, though the off-roading part is usually not on the list. That’s because the model is more of a fashion statement, a grocery getter, a school bus, and a daily, and since it is not on the affordable side of things, especially in the AMG G 63 configuration, which sits at the very top of the family, it does not get punished off the beaten path that often.
Mind you, one can easily take the modern-day Mercedes G-Wagen, regardless of the specification, for a quick drive off the lit path, though preferably after equipping it with a set of chunky tires for added grip. After all, this is still a body-on-frame truck, albeit one with a quite plush (for such a thing) interior, and an exterior that has aged like fine wine. But when again, why would it get thrashed when it costs a lot of money?
For instance, even the most basic version of the SUV will set you back a minimum of $153,900 for the latest model year in the United States of America. This is the MSRP of the Mercedes-Benz G 500 , which no longer features a V8, but a 3.0-liter inline-six turbocharged engine with mild-hybrid assistance. The mill is good for 443 hp (449 ps/330 kW) at 6,100 rpm and 413 lb-ft (560 Nm) of torque at 1,950-5,500 rpm, enabling 0-60 mph (0-97 kph) in 5.3 seconds.
Photo: Instagram | stars.in.the.ceiling Then comes the not-so-popular electric G-Class. Yes, the G-Wagen is also offered with a zero-emission powertrain, in case you forgot, and it is called the Mercedes-Benz G 580 . It starts at $163,750, has 579 hp (587 ps/432 kW) and 859 lb-ft (1,165 Nm) of torque combined from its four permanently synchronous electric motors, and takes 4.6 seconds to complete the 0-60 mph sprint.
Finally, the Mercedes-AMG G 63 sits at the top of the lineup, with an MSRP of $198,750, 0-60 mph in 4.2 seconds, and 577 hp (585 ps/430 kW) at 6,000 rpm and 627 lb-ft (850 Nm) of torque from 2,500 to 3,500 rpm from its 4.0-liter bi-turbo V8. It is this model that gets the most attention, and the configuration of the vehicle pictured in the gallery, which has been visited by the tuning fairy.
We would have probably ignored it, because the makeover is anything but dramatic. But then again, it has a famous owner. According to Stars In The Ceiling, which is the tuner behind it, this particular Mercedes-AMG G 63 is owned by Nicolas Batum. He is a former NBA player who recently retired, and he decided to spruce up his daily drives with a customized machine, hence why he turned to the quoted company.
The 37-year-old French former athlete’s Mercedes-AMG G 63 features a color-shifting wrap, and it is the thing that stands out the most on the outside. The wheels seem to have come from the aftermarket world, too. They are black, and spin around the red brake calipers. A chrome-delete package is part of the makeover, just like some plastic add-ons in the front bumper, and a few other tweaks on the outside.
Photo: Instagram | stars.in.the.ceiling Mind you, the tuner is not called Stars In The Ceiling for nothing, because this particular Mercedes G-Wagen also features a starry sky headliner, a feature that has become a bit too common in the tuning world these days. The lights are white, the headliner and pillars are black, and the leather upholstery on the seats, door cards, and probably other parts of the interior that are not visible in these pictures is presented in red, and looks OEM to us.
According to the tuner, the Alcantara steering wheel is new, and so are the ambient vents, and it is these that apparently round off the makeover, which is not bad at all, to be honest, as something like this always beats ordering a wacky body kit from a controversial tuner and having it installed on your G-Wagen. Thus, all we can do is congratulate Nicolas Batum for his fine machine, which has likely cost him a small fortune to modify.
Yeah, the pricing details have obviously not been revealed by Stars In The Ceiling, but then again, did you really think that the company would speak about the finances? Interested parties are being advised to reach out to the tuner for a makeover. And before wrapping it up, we have to ask you whether you dig the look of this modded Mercedes-AMG G 63 . So, do you? EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
Road-Legal XJ220 Scored Jaguar's Last Le Mans Win, Then Owned by Petro-Dollar Sultan, Is $6M Now
28 photos
Photo: Furlonger Specialist Cars
Remember Jaguar? The company that copies nothing, and has recently released one of the most controversial automobiles of this millennium. Ferrari’s Luce has stolen that spotlight (pun intended), but the British marque lacks a vital detail the Italian company abounds in: beautiful cars currently in production. Oh, how the mighty have fallen from the formidable XJ220 from the nineties…
Few machines from the 1990s supercar boom carry the mystique, controversy, and pedigree of the 1993 Jaguar XJ220C-LM. And bear in mind the Jag had some pretty strong rivals: Bugatti and McLaren were both going all-in, one with the EB110, the other with the F1. The Brits had to go big or go home. They went gigantic. And won Le Mans .
Currently offered for sale by Furlonger Specialist Cars in Ashford, Kent, displaying just 1,000 miles on its odometer and finished in factory Green over a Black interior, this machine, chassis 002, is one of the four endurance racing athletes. Jaguar produced 281 standard XJ220 road cars, which would be sufficient to put any example from that production run on a very high pedestal. This one, however, is above all.
What elevates chassis 002 from a static motorsport museum artifact to an automotive unicorn is its dual identity across track and street. Over recent months, specialists at Simon Furlonger conducted a comprehensive mechanical appraisal and completed the complex process required for official United Kingdom road registration. Because its underlying architecture shares core foundations with the street model, chassis 002 now stands as the only road-legal Jaguar XJ220C-LM in the world.
{fullimg}
To understand why the XJ220C-LM matters so deeply, we should revisit the dramatic shift in international endurance racing during the early 1990s. Following the demise of the Group C prototype era, production-based racing gained momentum worldwide as machines like the Ferrari F40 LM, Porsche 911 RSR, and Audi 90 GTO dominated North American IMSA competition. By 1993, organizers revived the Grand Touring category for the 24 Hours of Le Mans.
That revitalized class attracted 32 GT cars to the 1993 starting grid in France, prompting JaguarSport and Tom Walkinshaw Racing to transform Coventry's flagship supercar into a track weapon. Tom Walkinshaw Racing already boasted an illustrious endurance pedigree with Jaguar, having secured two historic overall victories at the 24 Hours of Le Mans alongside three World Sportscar Championships. Of the four XJ220C-LM cars constructed, Walkinshaw brought three to the French race.
Converting the opulent road coupe into a ruthless endurance contender demanded an aggressive weight-reduction program that shaved a full 400 kg (900 lb). Engineers discarded the production aluminum exterior skin and fitted completely detachable carbon-composite body panels engineered for rapid replacement during pit stops.
Photo: Furlonger Specialist Cars Furthermore, numerous structural aluminum components from the street car were replaced with bespoke race-grade carbon fiber and carbon-Kevlar composite parts for superior rigidity.
Mounted amidships is a Jaguar Group C-inspired 3.5-liter twin-turbocharged V6 engine derived from the Austin Rover V64V powerplant originally developed for the XJR-10 and XJR-11 prototypes. Displacing 3,498 cc with dual overhead camshafts and four valves per cylinder, this competition unit is capable of producing a staggering 850 hp (some 862 PS), far eclipsing the 542 bhp rating of the road car. Torque flows to the rear wheels through a 5-speed manual transaxle.
Sustaining 850 hp across a 24-hour endurance marathon (the car hit 213 mph / 343 kph in the race) required an extensively upgraded cooling package, enlarged heat exchangers, and revised aerodynamic ducting to manage extreme thermal loads. Underneath the composite bodywork, Tom Walkinshaw Racing installed fully adjustable competition suspension alongside an upgraded braking system engineered to haul the lightweight coupe down from speeds exceeding 200 mph.
Photo: Furlonger Specialist Cars Inside, the stripped-out Black cockpit replaces luxury leather trim with exposed structural carbon fiber throughout. When the quasi-works team arrived in France for the 24 Hours of Le Mans of 1993, chassis 002 served as the squad's lead entry wearing race number 50. Behind the wheel sat an elite trio comprising Danish endurance veteran John Nielsen, Australian sports car ace David Brabham, and rising Scottish talent David Coulthard (the future F1 driver, at his first - and only - Le Mans race).
Performing flawlessly while both sister cars retired, chassis 002 conquered the grueling contest to claim GT class victory. That celebration soon ignited a fierce regulatory dispute known as the catalytic converter appeal controversy. Because pre-race scrutineers questioned the absence of catalytic converters, the Jaguars were permitted to race under appeal.
Since the cars were entered under IMSA regulations that required no catalytic converters, the FIA ultimately upheld Jaguar's appeal, yet the ACO controversially ruled the paperwork late. Nevertheless, Brabham, Nielsen, and Coulthard kept their winners' trophies and credit.
Photo: Furlonger Specialist Cars Following its heroic performance at Le Mans in 1993, chassis 002 retired briefly to the Tom Walkinshaw Racing Museum collection before being acquired by the Sultan of Brunei. In 2000, the car returned to public view on loan for the traveling Jaguar Heritage display across major international venues.
Later, David Brabham reunited with chassis 002 at the 2011 Goodwood Festival of Speed before it joined an elite British racing collection.
Within the collector market, standard road-going XJ220 coupes typically trade around £550,000 (over $727k) in 2026, whereas genuine competition cars rarely surface for public sale. When chassis 001, a sister XJ220-C that retired early at Le Mans in 1993 and lacks road registration, crossed the auction block at Artcurial in 2020 and RM Sotheby's in 2021, it realized £913,938 ($1.2M) and £710,608 ($784K). However, winning Le Mans pedigree commands a vastly higher financial tier.
Photo: Furlonger Specialist Cars Auction records demonstrate the astronomical sums collectors pay for victorious Le Mans machinery. In February 2025, the 1965 Le Mans-winning 1964 Ferrari 250 LM, chassis 5893, sold through RM Sotheby's Paris for a record $36,344,960. Earlier benchmarks include the 1959 Le Mans-winning 1956 Aston Martin DBR1/1 that fetched $22,550,000 in 2017, the 1956-winning 1955 Jaguar D-Type XKD501 sold for $21,780,000 in 2016, and the 1983-winning 1982 Porsche 956-003 at $10,120,000.
Furlonger Specialist Cars lists this 1993 Jaguar XJ220C-LM with an asking price of £4,499,990, or €5,249,638 / $5,950,000. Viewed against the eight-figure scores mentioned above, chassis 002 is a bargain, at a fraction of those overall winners while offering something none can match: an 850 bhp Le Mans victor registered for public roads.

The Great Vansby Is a Camper Van With a Slide-Out Speakeasy — and It Sold for a Small Fortune
27 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Sandy Vans
Most camper vans are built to offer as much comfort and adventure capability as possible. That applies to the van I'm discussing today, but this one also has an interesting, distinctive purpose: to be able to host people.
Meet The Great Vansby, a custom project based on a Mercedes-Benz Sprinter with a 144" wheelbase. It was made by Sandy Vans, a San Diego, California-based company specializing in off-grid adventure conversions. We've covered some of its creations here on autoevolution, such as the Wabi camper van .
As usual, let's start by taking a look at the exterior. The vehicle rides on Agile Offroad wheels wrapped in BFGoodrich KO2 all-terrain tires. The tires are also equipped with Apex quick deflation valves.
Sandy Vans went even further to make sure this van can go off the beaten path. It installed Fox dual compression adjustable shocks in the front and back, a Stop the Sway kit with triple bypass shocks with a reservoir with a compression adjuster, and a big brake kit from Agile Offroad.
At the front, you'll come across a CAtuned bumper complete with two large amber light pods and a Smittybuilt winch rated for 12,000 lb. (5,447 kg). On the opposite end, the company fitted a Sandy Vans Boost Box for dirty gear, a swing-out bike rack that carries two e-bikes, and a spare tire carrier / ladder combo.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Sandy Vans A ladder mounted on the driver's side offers quick and easy access to the roof. There, you'll discover a Sandbar roof rack. It holds a Fiamma F45S awning with an integrated LED light, perimeter lights, a Starlink Mini antenna, and two 195 W solar panels.
Other notable mods are AMP Research automatic side steps, Sandy Vans storage lockers, and power and water hookups.
The inside is by far the more impressive part of the camper. Enter, and you'll be greeted by a beautifully designed interior. It has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space. What's more, the driver and passenger seats are mounted on swivel bases, allowing you to turn them around to face the back of the van.
Regarding aesthetics, you'll notice a bamboo slatted ceiling with recessed LED light strips, warm wood-imitating vinyl plank flooring, white wall panels, and cabinetry with a warm grain finish. The look is complemented by graphite grey textile upholstery and matte black fixtures.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Sandy Vans The first part of the living space is reserved for lounging and sleeping. It comprises two benches, one on each side of the interior, which have storage compartments accessible after lifting the cushions.
The bench on the passenger side also houses the van's highlight: a slide-out speakeasy that can be pulled out only when the sliding door is open. It includes a shaker, charcuterie knives, a holder for two glasses, and a folding panel that accommodates two extra glasses. These items can also be accessed by lifting the bench's hinged top.
On the opposite side, you'll find a larger bench that can double as a single bed. Furthermore, it accommodates the power system – its highlights are an 800 Ah lithium battery bank and a 3,000 W inverter. Three charging sources can help keep the batteries topped off: solar power , shore power, and DC-DC charging while the engine is running.
Above this area, you'll notice that the ceiling sits a bit lower than in the rest of the living space. Well, this isn't, in fact, the ceiling – it's actually the bottom part of a Lippert elevator bed made to resemble the van's ceiling.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Sandy Vans At the flip of a switch, you can bring down the elevator bed to your preferred position and go to sleep without having to set up the bed like you have to in other vans. You can also leave enough space underneath for a guest to sleep on the driver-side bench.
You can use a couple of storage spots while in bed, positioned in the top part of the cabin. Underneath them, Sandy Vans added a 32-inch flip-down TV that you can watch from pretty much anywhere in the van.
Walk further back inside the van, and you'll have the kitchen on the driver's side. It features a single-burner induction stovetop, a deep stainless steel sink with a cutting board cover, and some outlets. Several drawers, a lower cabinet, a pull-out spice rack, and a long overhead cabinet are available for storage in the kitchen.
The cool thing about the spice rack is that it holds a flip-up table on the side that faces the lounge, perfectly positioned to be used when sitting down on either bench.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Sandy Vans You get even more storage space on the opposite side thanks to a huge floor-to-ceiling unit. It offers a massive pantry with multiple shelves, a slide-out coffee maker, and a slide-out step with a removable top. Next to it, you'll discover a full-length fridge with a freezer compartment.
As for plumbing, the van is equipped with two water tanks (for fresh and grey water), a winterizing system, an accumulator, an Aqueous water heater, and an outdoor shower connection. Moreover, a slide-out tray houses a Laveo dry-flush toilet.
As expected from a premium build, this rig can handle four-season travel. It's equipped with a 12V rooftop A/C unit and a diesel-powered Espar heater that's tapped into the vehicle's fuel tank.
There is one more system that can make all the difference to an audiophile like me: an Alpine system with two speakers up front and a 12-inch subwoofer behind the driver's seat.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Sandy Vans All in all, The Great Vansby by Sandy Vans is an awesome creation that can take you off-road and off-grid and serve as the perfect gathering spot for you and your friends.
This camper van was sold for a whopping $280,000 (€252,551) – given the price of the AWD Sprinter platform and the amount of luxury this rig packs, the price isn't that surprising. It's still a small fortune, and I can't help but think that a fixed interior bathroom would've been nice – but that's just my preference.

Owner Parked His 1984 Chevrolet Corvette Under a Carport 25 Years Ago, Never Touched It Again
14 photos
Photo: Stauffer Garage | YouTube
The owner bought this 1984 Chevrolet Corvette 25 years ago, drove it home, and parked it under a carport right next to his house. He was planning to drive it, but then life got in the way, and he never touched it again. Over all these years, the black-painted C4 Corvette sat parked, collecting dust instead of miles. That explains why it looks like all car washes went into bankruptcy right now.
Now, the family has had enough of sitting and watching the 1984 C4 Corvette degrade in front of their eyes and called a detailer. That is how the ‘Vette ended up in the hands of James Stauffer of Stauffer Garage. He took on the challenge of making it look like it did the day it rolled off the production line of the General Motors Corvette Assembly Plant in Bowling Green, Kentucky, back in 1984.
The 1984 Corvette marked the debut of the fourth generation, which dropped as the model’s first complete ground-up redesign since 1968. Built as an extended 17-month production run, it transformed the Corvette from a cruiser into a high-tech, driver-focused sports car.
First and foremost, Chevrolet replaced the old body-on-frame architecture with a rigid "uniframe" chassis, which significantly improved handling, stiffness, and safety. Every 1984 Corvette featured a fighter-jet-inspired multicolored LCD instrument cluster with bar-graph tachometers and an onboard trip computer.
Photo: Stauffer Garage | YouTube Detailing starts with vacuuming away years of neglect from the fiberglass body before James proceeds to power washing and foaming to clean and decontaminate the black paint. He uses a microfiber towel to remove the grease and brushes to access the areas that are hard to reach.
Washing is far from enough He clay-bars the car to pull out the embedded microscopic dirt and grime from the vehicle’s clear coat that the regular washing left behind. Then he polishes to remove as much of the oxidation as possible, but he needs to be careful with the already fragile paint, battered by the elements for the past 25 years. The black paint is very demanding, and the car will need to be completely wet-sanded and resprayed to look good.
The cabin of the Chevy Corvette tells the exact same story as the exterior. Mold covers the seats, door panels, and the dashboard full of buttons, switches, and commuters, a layout designed to make you feel like you are sitting in a fighter jet cockpit rather than a car.
Expectedly, mice had turned the space into their own playground. While the survivors probably fled when they felt the car moving, they left behind their deceased relatives that now look ready for a high school biology class.
Photo: Stauffer Garage | YouTube .
The seats wrapped in black perforated leather have started to show their age, as they display the typical wear and tear. No surprise there! A special mix and the stain extractor remove the dirt embedded in the black carpets, which have aged well.
With an all-purpose cleaner and brushes to agitate the dirt and take it out from inside the seams, James gets rid of years of neglect. At the end of the day, the car is a huge step closer to its former glory. The car doesn’t run and doesn’t drive, but someone else will have to fix that.
A single engine option The 1984 Chevrolet Corvette is powered by the 350-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) L83 V8 engine, carried over from the 1982 C3 Corvette and exclusive to the 1984 model year of the C4 generation before General Motors replaced it with the Tuned Port Injection L98 V8 in 1985.
The 350 V8 pumps out 205 horsepower (208 metric horsepower) and 290 pound-feet of torque for a run from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 7.1 seconds with the auto box or 6.4 seconds with the manual transmission, which is the case for this car. The C4 Corvette could hit 142 mph (229 kph) in a straight line with the right pedal down.
Photo: Stauffer Garage | YouTube The Doug Nash “4+3” manual transmission with computer-controlled overdrive on the top three gears puts the power down through the rear wheels in pure Corvette fashion, coming from an era when General Motors was still light-years away from rolling out a hybrid all-wheel-drive Corvette.
Back in 1984, the Chevrolet Corvette was a $21,800 deal. The base MSRP made it the first-ever Corvette to cross the $20,000 mark. Adjusted for inflation, that would be roughly $69,200 today. That is just $3,000 under what General Motors is asking for a brand-new Corvette Stingray in 2026.
However, those in the market for a C4 Corvette could find one for as little as $4,000 if high mileage, occasional mechanical gremlins, and faded paint aren't dealbreakers. At the opposite end of the C4 Corvette used car market sit delivery-mileage, museum pieces with original window stickers and untouched interiors, selling for over $20,000.

33-Year-Old Drives Around With a Bugatti Chiron in Pokémon-Inspired Livery, Still Flies Economy
15 photos
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube
A young entrepreneur has just bought a 2019 Bugatti Chiron. Instead of locking it in a climate-controlled garage and only taking it out for maintenance, he feels like he has to give back. Down-to-earth and generous, he lets people who look at his car sit in it and take photos.
Yucong "Jesse" Peng is a tech entrepreneur, real estate investor, and ultra-high-end Pokémon collector. He owns one of Canada's largest personal Pokémon card collections, valued in the multi-seven-figure range, and claims to hold the world's largest collection of Suicune cards. Alongside his wife, he co-owns Vancity CJ, a well-known Pokémon card shop in Richmond, British Columbia.
He really wanted a Bugatti Chiron , and there were only two for sale in Canada. He originally chose another, until a friend of his told him to back out because it was a lemon. So he ended up buying the only other car on the market at the time.
It came with a perfectly clean background, had just 1,119 miles (1,800 kilometers) on the clock at the time, and it is still under extended warranty until April 2027. So, he negotiated a bit and decided to buy it sight unseen.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube He wired the money about a month ago, and then it took the seller three weeks to ship it to Vancouver. Right after delivery, he had to go on a business trip and kept thinking about going back home and driving his new Chiron .
It is finished in dark blue with contrasting light blue accents and has the Mega Charizard X on both doors. It comes as an addition to his fleet, which also includes a Lamborghini Urus with a Mega Charizard Y on the side.
He recalls that when he moved to the U.S. at the age of six, he was a nerdy little kid who didn’t speak English at all. He didn't have any friends, so he got into Pokémon. So he started making friends who had the same hobby and started learning the language. It was the hobby that got him to meet his wife. " I feel like I owe it everything I've got ," he says.
He doesn’t mind people staring at his car and inquiring about it. He actually opens the door to them and lets them sit in it. Jesse is doing everything he can to help those who didn't have the opportunity to buy their dream cars and is also doing a lot for cancer research.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube Over the past year, he has become very close to the family of Avery Liam Garcia Valentin, known as Avery the Poke Kid. He passed away on September 18, 2026, at the age of 12, after a tough eight-year battle with a rare form of pancreatic cancer.
Jesse is by no means the kind of owner who would put this car in a climate-controlled garage and never touch it again. He plans to drive it and make it worth every cent. He can actually afford just about any car out there, but he still flies economy.
He was actually planning to buy a Lamborghini Reventon with 640 horsepower (650 metric horsepower) for about $2.5 million. However, he ended up getting a Chiron with 1,479 horsepower (1,500 metric horsepower) and 1,180 pound-feet (1,600 Newton meters) of torque, coming out of a massive 8.0-liter quad-turbocharged W16 .
Those numbers make it flash from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 2.3 seconds, run the quarter mile in 9.4 seconds, and max out at 261 mph (420 kph). A seven-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission puts the power down through all four corners.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube To Jesse, however, the Bugatti Chiron he has just bought is not about speed and sheer power. It is about how far the Chinese kid with no friends has made it and the work he has put into it over the years and about keeping his head down.
" I have been blessed to own supercars for the past eight years of my life ," Jesse says, but none of them compares to his Bugatti. " It doesn't feel real! " For him, it all comes down to passion, discipline, and motivation. He is the complete opposite of a party guy and prefers to spend time focusing on his business.
He doesn't take shortcuts to success and prefers to think long-term in " a short-term world. " He spends money on his passions, but also for his loved ones. This year, he also bought his parents a house and their dream RV.
It doesn't feel real for TJ Lamb of Magnacars, who gets to drive Jesse's Chiron. He is overwhelmed by the road behavior, but the drive is far from perfect. The visibility is terrible in the French hypercar. That’s probably why you see more Toyotas than Bugattis on the road, right?
Luckily, Jesse is in the passenger seat and keeps an eye on traffic to cover up for the huge blind spot he has to deal with.
